# Venous and Arterial Thrombosis Associated with Abemaciclib Therapy for Metastatic Breast Cancer

**Authors:** Nathan W. Watson; Seth A. Wander; Joseph J. Shatzel; Hanny Al-Samkari

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 2Division of Hematology Oncology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA | 3Knight Cancer Institute, Oregon Health and Sciences University, Portland, OR | 4Division of Biomedical Engineering, Oregon Health and Sciences University, Portland, OR

## Abstract

The CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib is a mainstay of treatment for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer. However, increased venous thromboembolism (VTE) rates in multiple clinical trials resulted in a black box warning for this agent. Thrombosis rates in unselected real-world populations receiving abemaciclib remain ill-defined.

We conducted a multicenter observational cohort study of patients with metastatic breast cancer receiving abemaciclib. The primary endpoint was thrombosis during treatment or within 30 days of discontinuation. Multivariable logistic models assessed predictors of VTE and a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model assessed mortality.

364 patients were included, with a median treatment duration of 5.5 months. Twenty-six patients developed 27 (7.4%) thrombotic events (17 VTE, 9 arterial thrombosis, and 1 with both events). No baseline characteristics were associated with increased VTE risk in multivariable modeling. Patients developing VTE during therapy had a higher risk of death than those who did not (HR 2.09, 95% CI, 1.07–4.13). Median survival in patients who developed VTE versus those who did not was 9.6 vs. 25.8 months, respectively. The rate of VTE and any thrombosis during abemaciclib therapy was 9.1 and 13.7 events per 100 person-years, respectively, notably higher than rates observed in clinical trials.

In a real-world setting, abemaciclib was associated with a VTE rate approximately two-fold greater than the already elevated rates reported in the MONARCH trials. Patients developing thrombosis on abemaciclib had a significantly higher risk of death. Given these findings, studies evaluating the role of thromboprophylaxis in patients receiving abemaciclib are needed.

In this multicenter observational cohort study of patients with metastatic breast cancer receiving abemaciclib, we demonstrate that abemaciclib is associated with a VTE rate approximately two-fold greater than the already elevated rates reported in the MONARCH 2 and 3 clinical trials. These findings in an unselected real-world population indicate that future studies evaluating the role of thromboprophylaxis for abemaciclib are needed.

## INTRODUCTION

Breast cancer is the most common malignancy of women, affecting 1 in 8 women in the United States.1,2 Hormone receptor (HR)-positive breast cancer is the most common subtype, encompassing 70% of patients diagnosed with metastatic disease.3,4 Endocrine-based therapy (ET) is the mainstay approach to treatment for such patients; however, disease progression is often inevitable due to the eventual development of acquired resistance.5,6 Over the past several years, inhibitors of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK 4/6) have emerged as a new therapeutic strategy for the treatment of HR-positive breast cancer.7,8 CDK 4/6 inhibitors are oral, highly selective, small molecule inhibitors of the CDK 4 and 6 proteins shown to inhibit cell cycle progression and arrest cells in the G1 phase.9 Currently, there are three CDK 4/6 inhibitors approved by the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) primarily for use in combination therapy for advanced disease.10

The first FDA-approved CDK 4/6 inhibitor was palbociclib (Ibrance®, Pfizer).11–13 Palbociclib in combination with ET demonstrated a superior survival benefit in pivotal phase III trials compared with ET alone and was approved for use in the metastatic disease setting.14 However, as with other targeted therapies15, increased venous thromboembolism (VTE) rates have been reported with this agent. In a recent meta-analysis pooling data from the PALOMA-1, 2, and 3 trials, VTE occurred in 1.6% of patients while on palbociclib therapy.16 Recent studies have additionally suggested an even higher VTE incidence of approximately 6–10% in real-world populations receiving palbociclib rather than highly selected clinical trial populations.17–19

Two additional CDK 4/6 inhibitors have been approved for this patient population: ribociclib (Kisqali®, Novartis) and abemaciclib (Verzenio®, Eli Lilly).20–24 Abemaciclib’s current FDA label for HR-positive metastatic disease is based on evidence established from the MONARCH family of clinical trials. More recently, abemaciclib has become the first and only CDK 4/6 inhibitor to date to expand its current indications beyond the metastatic disease setting in breast cancer.25 It is also the only CDK 4/6 inhibitor with an approval for use as monotherapy. The recently completed monarchE trial demonstrated a mortality benefit for abemaciclib used with endocrine therapy for early, high-risk disease.26

Despite the favorable efficacy established in these trials, high incidences of VTE have been reported in clinical trials for abemaciclib.27 In MONARCH 2, VTE occurred in 21 patients (4.8%) receiving abemaciclib compared to 2 patients receiving placebo and was the most frequently reported serious adverse event.23 MONARCH 3 reported an even higher 6% VTE incidence, an approximate 10-fold higher incidence than placebo.24 Taken together, this evidence has resulted in a black box warning for increased VTE risk on abemaciclib’s current FDA label. Notably, a high rate of thromboembolic events was also observed in clinical trials of ribociclib as well with 23 patients (4.8%) experiencing pulmonary embolism after receiving this agent in the MONALESSA 3 study.28

Given that clinical trials select for patients with limited comorbidities and a good performance status, the potential risk of thromboembolism with abemaciclib may be higher in a real-world setting, similar to what has been observed with palbociclib. Because even higher rates of thromboembolism have been observed in clinical trials of abemaciclib as compared with palbociclib, understanding the rates in real-world practice is crucial for this agent. This is critically important to inform both CDK4/6 agent selection as well as consideration of thromboprophylaxis. To date, data describing the thrombosis risk of abemaciclib in real-world clinical practice are limited. In this multicenter, observational cohort study, we evaluate the real-world rates and predictors of venous and arterial thrombosis in patients receiving abemaciclib for metastatic breast cancer.

## METHODS

### Patients and Data Collection

This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Partners Healthcare (approval number 2020P003983). We conducted a multicenter observational cohort study of patients with metastatic breast cancer receiving abemaciclib. A research patient data repository containing patient data at five affiliated hospitals was queried to identify all patients receiving abemaciclib. Patients were excluded if breast cancer was not their primary diagnosis or if abemaciclib was received as part of a clinical trial. Data was collected from patients beginning therapy between November 1, 2017 and December 1, 2020. The date of database lock was April 29, 2021. A manual chart review was utilized to extract all data. We collected patient data including demographics, concurrent medications, laboratory studies at time of treatment, Khorana risk score, and tumor characteristics including histology, tumor expression patterns, and sites of metastasis. Relevant venous and arterial thrombotic risk factors including age, BMI, prior thrombosis, recent surgery, hereditary thrombophilia, systemic inflammatory diseases, presence of brain metastases, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and known atherosclerosis were collected for all patients. Systemic autoimmune disease included known history of connective tissue disease (such as systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, seronegative spondyloarthritis, or others) and inflammatory bowel disease. Known thrombophilia included known history of factor V Leiden, the prothrombin gene G20210A mutation, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, protein C deficiency, protein S deficiency, or antithrombin III deficiency. The primary endpoint of this study was venous and/or arterial thrombosis during abemaciclib treatment or within 30 days of discontinuation. Data are presented as either median (IQR) or number of patients (%).

All symptomatic and asymptomatic venous and arterial thrombotic events were included in this study. Venous thromboembolic events included upper and lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT), splanchnic vein thrombosis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, superficial thrombophlebitis, and pulmonary embolism. Arterial thrombotic events included ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), unstable angina, ischemic stroke (with or without hemorrhagic conversion), transient ischemic attack (TIA), peripheral arterial thrombosis, and mesenteric artery thrombosis. All venous thromboembolic events were confirmed based on current standard-of-care diagnostic imaging methods including but not limited to ultrasound or CT imaging where applicable. Acute coronary events including STEMI, NSTEMI, and unstable angina were confirmed based on cardiac biomarker clinical criteria as well as electrocardiogram evidence of ischemia or infarction. Stroke was confirmed based on current standard-of-care cross-sectional brain imaging including CT and/or MRI. Venous or arterial thrombosis was considered associated with abemaciclib if it occurred during therapy or within 30 days of discontinuation.

### Statistical Analysis

Predictors of VTE were selected a priori and assessed in a multivariable logistic model including age, race, BMI, receipt of long-term anticoagulation, receipt of aspirin, brain metastases, Khorana risk score, receipt of tamoxifen, prior VTE, systemic autoimmune disease, and known thrombophilia as independent variables. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was used to compare survival in patients developing VTE with those who did not. The model included age, race, HER2 status, receipt of long-term anticoagulation, receipt of aspirin, brain metastases, Khorana risk score, receipt of tamoxifen, prior VTE, systemic autoimmune disease, and known thrombophilia as independent variables.

Rates of VTE and any thrombotic event expressed in person-years were compared between the present cohort and the MONARCH 2 and 3 studies. These rates were calculated by dividing the total number of thrombotic events observed by the total time at risk, the latter of which was calculated by multiplying the median duration of abemaciclib treatment with the number of patients. This approach was taken for both the present cohort and MONARCH 2 and 3 studies because the total duration at risk for the MONARCH 2 and 3 studies is not available. To maintain consistency with our definition of abemaciclib-associated thrombosis, for the present cohort, the duration of exposure for each patient was defined as the duration of time on therapy plus 30 days after discontinuation.

Statistical analysis and figures were prepared using Stata version 14.2 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX), GraphPad Prism 7 (GraphPad, Inc., San Diego, CA), and Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corp., Seattle, WA).

## RESULTS

### Patient Cohort and Tumor Characteristics

A total of 397 patients were identified in our database query, of which 33 patients did not meet inclusion criteria and were excluded (Figure 1). 364 patients were included in our study.

Table 1 summarizes the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of included patients. 360 (98.9%) patients identified as female and had a median age of 61 (53–71) years. The majority of patients were postmenopausal at the initiation of abemaciclib (320 patients, 88.7%). Patients were mostly white (87.9%) and most had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 (45.4%) or 1 (37.4%). Abemaciclib was frequently administered concurrently with endocrine therapy (80.0%) of which fulvestrant was the most utilized agent (48.1%). 19 total patients (5.2%) were on concomitant tamoxifen therapy.

At the time of abemaciclib initiation, 51 patients (14%) were recipients of long-term anticoagulation and 47 patients (12.9%) were recipients of long-term antiplatelet therapy in the form of aspirin; no patients were receiving dipyridamole or a P2Y12 inhibitor. Direct oral anticoagulants were the most frequently utilized anticoagulant (31 patients, 8.5%). Patients had Khorana risk scores at the time of treatment initiation ranging between 0–3 with a skew towards low scores: 339 patients (93.1%) had a score of 0 or 1. The median duration of abemaciclib therapy was 5.5 (2.8–13.0) months. The median duration of follow-up was 12.7 (6.2–22.1) months.

Table 2 highlights the disease characteristics for patients included in our cohort. 267 patients (73.4%) and 46 patients (12.6%) had invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, respectively. Nearly all patients had tumors that were estrogen receptor (ER) positive (99.5%) and 78.3% of tumors were also progesterone receptor (PR) positive. Brain metastases were frequent at the time of initiating therapy and present in 19.5% of patients.

### Thrombotic Events

26 total patients developed 27 thrombotic events during abemaciclib therapy or within 30 days of discontinuation. Events are described in detail in Table 3. 17 patients (4.7%) had a VTE, 9 patients had an arterial thrombosis (2.5%), and 1 patient had both events (0.3%). The median time to any thrombotic event while on abemaciclib was 2.8 months. The median time to VTE while on abemaciclib was also 2.8 months. The most common VTE attributed to abemaciclib was PE which occurred in 7 total patients (1.9%). Three additional patients (0.8%) had a concurrent DVT and PE. The most common arterial thrombotic event was stroke occurring in 4 total patients (1.1%). One patient (0.3%) had both a VTE and arterial thrombosis while on abemaciclib therapy. This patient had a pulmonary embolism and stroke which occurred on the same day and was recorded as a single thrombotic event. Another patient had both a TIA and stroke each occurring at separate time points and requiring separate hospitalizations for management.

One patient developed thrombosis while on prophylactic-dose enoxaparin prescribed for a prior pulmonary embolism. This patient presented with advanced metastatic disease and was found on admission to have multi-focal strokes and ultimately expired from complications of these events shortly after discharge. Additionally, two patients had arterial thrombosis while on prophylactic-dose aspirin. Similarly, both patients had advanced disease on presentation and were found to have large strokes with one patient having additional clot burden in the left ventricle without a prior diagnosis of atrial fibrillation.

### Rates of VTE and Total Thrombosis

The rate of VTE in the present cohort was 9.1 per 100 person-years, compared with rates of 4.1 and 4.9 events per 100 person-years calculated from the MONARCH 2 and 3 trials, respectively.23,24 The rate of total thrombosis including both VTE and arterial thrombosis in this cohort was 13.7 per 100 person-years, compared with rates of 4.1 and 4.9 events per 100 person-years calculated from the MONARCH 2 and 3 trials, respectively (no arterial thrombotic events were reported in either of these clinical trials).23,24

### Risk Factors for VTE

Relevant risk factors for venous and arterial thrombosis were collected and illustrated in Table 4. 18.4% of patients had a previous history of VTE and 5.8% had a prior history of arterial thrombosis. Known thrombophilia was present in 5 total patients, 4 of which had antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and 1 had Factor V Leiden. The most common risk factors for arterial thrombosis were hypertension and hyperlipidemia occurring in 44.5% and 35.7% of the cohort, respectively.

A multivariable logistic model utilized to assess for risk factors of VTE did not find any associations of baseline characteristics with increased VTE risk.

### Survival

At the time of analysis, 225 patients (61.8%) were alive. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was performed to compare patients with and without any thrombosis, VTE only, and arterial thrombosis only (Figure 2). Median survival in patients developing any thrombosis (venous or arterial) vs. those who did not was 25.8 months and 26.7 months, respectively. In a multivariable Cox model controlling for 10 disease and thrombosis-relevant covariates, patients developing VTE during abemaciclib therapy had a significantly higher risk of death (hazard ratio, 2.09, 95% CI, 1.07–4.13, P=0.032). Median overall survival in patients developing a VTE vs. those who did not was 9.6 months vs. 25.8 months, respectively (Figure 2B). Arterial thrombosis was not associated with reduced survival in our cohort (Figure 2C).

Of the twelve patients who died following thrombosis, death was likely attributed to the thrombosis in three patients (25%) and possibly related to the thrombosis in three more (25%). The six (50%) remaining patients died secondary to disease progression apparently unrelated to thrombosis.

## DISCUSSION

In this multicenter observational cohort study of 364 patients with metastatic breast cancer, we provide the first real-world data describing the risk of venous and arterial thrombosis in patients treated with the CDK 4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib. Prior to this study, the largest number of patients treated with abemaciclib in a real-world cohort study evaluating thromboembolism was, to the best of our knowledge, just 37 patients.17 We found a high incidence of thromboembolism associated with abemaciclib treatment in our study, with 7.4% of patients developing thromboembolic complications during abemaciclib therapy over a median treatment duration of just 5.5 months. The median time to thrombosis in patients developing a thrombotic event was just 2.8 months after initiating abemaciclib therapy.

As this study was conducted in real-world clinical practice, our cohort differed from the highly selected MONARCH trial populations where much of the thrombosis risk of abemaciclib was originally described23,24,29 in ways that could both increase and decrease thrombotic risk. Firstly, 14.1% of our cohort was on long-term anticoagulation and 12.9% of patients were on long-term antiplatelet therapy while receiving abemaciclib, high rates of pre-existing antithrombotic therapy that could have diminished overall thrombotic risk. While the MONARCH 2 and 3 trial populations did not specifically exclude patients on long-term antithrombotic therapy, they did exclude patients with certain forms of cardiovascular disease23,24, which likely reduced antithrombotic therapy use in enrolled patients. Second, our cohort had a notably high proportion of patients with prior thrombotic events: 18.4% of patients had a history of VTE and 5.8% had a history of arterial thrombosis. Finally, our cohort had a high prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors, strongly increasing the risk of arterial thrombosis. The risk factors represented at the highest rates include hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and atrial fibrillation. MONARCH 2 and 3 excluded patients with certain types of cardiovascular disease, which may have contributed to the absence of arterial thrombotic events in both of these studies.

The high incidences of VTE reported in MONARCH 2 and 3 (4.8% and 6.1%, respectively) earned the drug a black box warning from the U.S. FDA for VTE risk.24,30 Our study confirms this labeling is not only warranted but that the thrombotic rates in real-world populations appear to be even higher. In consideration of thrombotic event rates in person-years, we observed an approximately three-fold increase in any thrombosis and two-fold increase in VTE compared with the MONARCH trials. Notably, no arterial thrombosis events were reported in either MONARCH 2 or 3 over a median duration of ≥14 months of abemaciclib therapy, possibly reflective of a highly selected trial population; conversely, our cohort had rates of cardiovascular risk factors as would be expected in a cohort with a median age of 63 years and found a worrisome 2.5% arterial thrombosis incidence over a median of just 5.5 months of abemaciclib therapy. As abemaciclib is often prescribed in combination with aromatase inhibitors or tamoxifen, it also is worth considering the added thromboembolic risk of these agents as well. While tamoxifen has a well-established venous thromboembolic risk profile31, the risks for steroidal and non-steroidal aromatase inhibitors appear to be considerably lower as demonstrated in multiple trials comparing their use to tamoxifen.32,33 To account for this known VTE risk for tamoxifen in this study, we controlled for tamoxifen use in the multivariable analysis.

Importantly, while we did not find any clinical or tumor-associated characteristics that predicted for thrombosis on multivariable modeling, we did find that development of VTE while on abemaciclib therapy was associated with an approximate two-fold increase in mortality risk, with a much lower overall survival. This association was demonstrated utilizing a multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression controlling for 10 relevant covariates. Notably, in two prior retrospective studies investigating thrombosis rates in patients receiving palbociclib, neither found a statistically significant increase in mortality due to VTE.17,18 The reasons for these disparate findings are not clear.

Our findings are particularly important at present as abemaciclib has recently become the first and only CDK 4/6 inhibitor to date to be approved for use beyond the metastatic disease setting. In the recently completed monarchE study, abemaciclib was found to extend invasive disease-free survival in patients with early, high-risk HR-positive breast cancer. Although VTE was reported in fewer patients (2.3%) in monarchE, patients treated with abemaciclib had VTE at an incidence approximately five times that of placebo.26 As abemaciclib use continues to extend to more patients with HR-positive breast cancer, the role of thromboprophylaxis continues to remain uncertain. Risk stratification for primary thromboprophylaxis in patients with malignancy is done most commonly utilizing the well-validated Khorana risk score.34 In this study and prior studies examining thrombotic complications of CDK4/6 inhibitors,17 the Khorana score did not predict for the development of VTE in patients on these agents. Given the considerable rates of thrombosis observed in both the clinical trials and this real-world setting over relatively short exposure intervals (suggesting the possibility of higher rates with more prolonged exposure), it is likely that low-risk thromboprophylaxis strategies (i.e. aspirin 81 mg daily or prophylactic-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban) could be beneficial for certain patient subgroups, or perhaps even unselected populations receiving abemaciclib therapy. However, dedicated studies are obviously necessary to quantify the risk and benefit of both unselected and targeted thromboprophylaxis.

Our study has a number of strengths but also important limitations. We report on a large number of patients. Rather than relying on administrative or claims data, we undertook laborious and comprehensive manual chart review of all patients to ensure the accuracy of all pulled data, including thromboembolic events and risk factors for thrombosis. The limitations of our work are primarily due to the observational nature of the study design and the lack of a comparator group. As is the case in all retrospective studies, it is always possible, albeit unlikely, that certain events may not have been captured due to the patient seeking care at another institution. Additionally, we relied on calculated approximate durations at risk for the MONARCH trials in our comparison of thrombotic rates, as the total duration at risk for those trials is not available. Finally, it is worth noting that similar to other real-world studies investigating patients with breast cancer,35,36 our cohort was primarily composed of white women, potentially limiting the generalizability of these results to non-white patients.

In summary, we found an approximate three-fold higher rate of thrombosis with abemaciclib treatment in a real-world population as compared with clinical trials. The median duration to thrombosis was less than 3 months after starting abemaciclib. In a multivariable Cox model controlling for relevant covariates, patients developing VTE had an approximate 2-fold risk of mortality. Given these findings, studies evaluating the role of thromboprophylaxis in patients receiving abemaciclib are needed.
